Kolosnitsyn2 | Damla Eroglu1 1Department of Chemical Engineering, Bogazici University, Istanbul, Turkey | 2Department of Electrochemical Energy, Ufa Institute of Chemistry – Subdivision of the Ufa Federal Research Centre of the Russian Academy of Sciences (UIC UFRC RAS), Ufa, Russia Correspondence: Damla Eroglu (eroglud@bogazici.edu.tr) Received: 24 February 2026 | Revised: 20 April 2026 | Accepted: 23 April 2026 Keywords: E/S ratio | electrochemistry | electrolyte design | lithium-sulfur battery | voltammetry ABSTRACT Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries are among the most promising next-generation battery technologies due to their high theoretical specific capacity.
Li-S battery performance is intricately linked to materials and cell design, with electrolyte design playing a particularly crucial role owing to the complex mechanisms within the cell.

Thus, the primary challenge in realizing highperformance Li-S batteries lies in achieving reasonable capacities and cycling performance at low electrolyte-to-sulfur (E/S) ratios, which might be attainable through unconventional electrolyte systems.
This study aims to explore how varying the amount and composition of electrolytes affects the performance of Li-S batteries across different electrolyte systems.
Sulfolane (SL)-Lithium bis(trifluoromethane)sulfonimide (LiTFSI) and triglyme (G3)-LiTFSI electrolytes demonstrate superior cycling performance across a range of E/S ratios.

Notably, the SL-LiTFSI electrolyte system shows promise under lean electrolyte conditions, demonstrating superior performance at the lowest E/S ratio of 6 mL g−1, likely due to sulfolane’s electrochemical stability, high dielectric constant, and donor number. 1 | Introduction Lithium-ion batteries are among the most widely used electrochemical storage technologies in various sectors, especially transportation.
Even though Li-ion batteries have high energy and power densities and long life, they have high costs and limited capacity for newly emerging technologies such as electric vehicles [1–3].
Consequently, researchers seek new battery systems with higher capacity and lower cost.

Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries have recently been a top research topic on next-generation energy storage technologies due to their high theoretical specific energy that is three to fivefold (nearly 2600 Wh/kg) of Li-ion batteries and the high theoretical specific capacity, 1675 mAh g−1, of their cathode active material, sulfur [4–9].
In addition to this, sulfur is low-cost, naturally abundant, and nontoxic [10–13].
However, due to the complicated mechanisms within Li-S cells during cycling, several challenges must be handled before commercialization.
One of the biggest obstacles is the shuttling of the lithium polysulfides (LiPSs) produced by the complex reactions in the cell [12, 14–16].
This shuttle mechanism leads to vital problems, such as the deterioration of the anode and loss of active cathode material [17, 18].

In addition to the polysulfide shuttle mechanism, the instability of the Li metal and the insulating nature of S and the final discharge product Li2S, hindering the reaction kinetics, are major concerns.
All these obstacles give rise to capacity fading, deficient coulombic efficiency, and short cycle life [1, 19–22].

There are different approaches in the literature to overcome these challenges, including engineering the cathode [4, 23–26], using a protective layer on the anode surface [27–29], and modifying the separator [30–34].
One critical approach to improving battery performance is electrolyte design, as the electrolyte type, properties, and amount Kagan Yuksel and Ayca Firtin contributed equally to this study.

control the dissolution of the polysulfides and, thus, the reaction and polysulfide shuttle mechanisms.

Consequently, the ideal electrolyte should be chemically and electrochemically stable across a wide range of voltage and temperature, have high ionic conductivity (10−3 to 10−2 S cm−1 at room temperature), compatibility with the Li metal, and low viscosity [35].
Therefore, the selection of the electrolyte components is highly determinative of battery performance.
Conventionally, ether-based electrolytes are used in the cell due to their compatibility with the cathode, low viscosity, and stability toward the polysulfides.
However, in ether-based electrolytes, the shuttle effect is severe, and the rapid evaporation of solvent causes safety concerns [36].
The most commonly used electrolyte system in Li-S batteries is 1 M lithium bis(trifluoromethane)sulfonomide (LiTFSI) in 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) and 1,2-dimethoxy ethane (DME) mixture (1:1 vol%).
DOL:DME exhibits excellent polysulfide solubility and strong chemical stability against polysulfides [36].
DME, a polar solvent with higher polysulfide solubility, provides high polysulfide kinetics but is more likely to react with lithium.
DOL reduces polysulfide solubility but aids in creating a more stable solid electrolyte interface (SEI) on the lithium anode surface [36].
A mixture of DOL:DME offers a compromise between electrolyte characteristics such as ionic conductivity, polysulfide solubility, mobility, and the generation of an SEI on the lithium anode.
However, the ether solvents’ low flash point creates a variety of safety concerns, mainly when operating at higher temperatures [36, 37].
The salt used in the electrolyte should have high ionic conductivity and not lead to unwanted side reactions with the LiPSs.
LiTFSI, the most widely used salt in Li-S battery electrolytes, enhances the electrolyte’s electrochemical stability and ionic conductivity.
Lithium trifluoromethanesulfonate (LiTF) and lithium perchlorate (LiClO4) are alternative salts that can be used in electrolyte design.
The former helps the solubility of shorterlength LiPSs and has high thermal stability, while the latter acts as a prohibitor of the polysulfide shuttle mechanism [38–40].
As for the solvents, they should have high solubility for short-chain polysulfides and poor solubility for long-chain polysulfides.
Triglyme (G3) is a promising candidate as a solvent since it has high polysulfide solubility and is chemically stable against polysulfides [41].
Also, it has lower flammability, flash point, and toxicity than the conventional electrolyte [42].
Another promising electrolyte solvent is sulfolane (SL), which can solve the shorter-length polysulfides formed during cycling owing to its high dielectric constant.
Sulfolane is also thermally stable and has a high boiling point and chemical stability, allowing the use of reactive salts [38, 43].

In addition to electrolyte components, the electrolyte-to-sulfur (E/S) ratio is also a crucial parameter for electrolyte design because it considerably affects the electrochemical performance and system- and cell-level-specific energy and energy density of the Li-S batteries.
Also, the E/S ratio plays a significant role in the reactions and the polysulfide shuttle mechanism because of its effect on the polysulfide concentration on the cathode surface [44–46].

At very low E/S ratios, the discharge capacity and cycling performance are poor; an increase in the electrolyte viscosity due to the rising polysulfide concentration results in lower ionic conductivity and poor reaction kinetics.
Moreover, low E/S ratios may lead to a deficiency of the electrolyte in the cell due to Li metal consuming the electrolyte via unwanted reactions [47].
An increase in the electrolyte amount impacts the voltage, cycle life, and capacity of the cell favorably by improving sulfur utilization and reaction kinetics.
However, a further increase in the E/S ratio adversely affects capacity retention since it may accelerate the polysulfide shuttle mechanism.
High electrolyte amounts also diminish the energy density [8, 35, 45, 46, 48–55].
Recently, we developed electrochemical models to reveal the impact of E/S ratio and electrolyte type on battery performance [56].
To achieve high energy density at the pack level, which is critical for commercializing these batteries, the E/S ratio should be minimized within the cell.
However, as discussed, battery performance decreases severely with decreasing electrolyte amount for the conventional electrolyte system [47, 55, 57–62].

Therefore, the bottleneck of achieving high-performance Li-S batteries is to attain reasonable capacities and cycling performance at low E/S ratios, which may be possible using electrolyte systems differing from the conventional one [61, 62].

In this regard, this study aims to mechanistically investigate the effect of the electrolyte amount and components on the performance of Li-S batteries with different electrolyte systems. 2 | Results and Discussion Figure 1 shows the cycling performance of Li-S batteries with various electrolyte systems, SL-LiTFSI, SL-LiTF, SL-LiClO4, G3-LiTFSI, and G3-LiTF, at four different E/S ratios.
At higher E/S ratios and flooded conditions, cells exhibit initial discharge capacities above 800 mAh g−1.
It is observed that Li-S batteries containing SL-LiTFSI and G3-LiTFSI electrolytes demonstrate superior cycling performance compared to other electrolytes at almost all E/S ratios.
This superiority may be attributed to the perfect cycling stability and rate capability of the LiTFSI [63].
Despite these benefits, LiTFSI may lead to higher viscosity, decreasing ionic conductivity [38, 63–65], especially at low E/S ratios, exacerbating the polysulfide shuttle mechanism [50, 51].
This is apparent in Figure 1d, particularly in the G3-LiTFSI electrolyte; at an E/S ratio of 6 mL g−1, the cell with G3-LiTFSI shows inferior performance.

The cycling performance of the Li-S cell with SL-LiTFSI is better than that of G3-LiTFSI, most probably due to the electrochemical stability, high dielectric constant, and donor number of sulfolane [38, 63, 66].

Sulfolane-based electrolytes have higher coulombic efficiencies (CEs) at all E/S ratios around 90%, whereas glyme-based electrolytes have lower and noisier CEs, demonstrating the high amount of shuttling in Figure S1.

Even though LiClO4 has been reported to result in high coulombic efficiency and suppress the shuttle effect [40, 46, 65], cells with the SL-LiClO4 electrolyte exhibit the lowest discharge capacity for almost all E/S ratios (except for 16 mL g−1).
While the cycling performance of Li-S cells with SL-LiTFSI is not affected by the alteration of the E/S ratio, a change in the E/S ratio affects the performance of the other electrolytes.
In particular, G3-LiTF shows the best discharge capacity and capacity retention at the lowest E/S ratio of 6 mL g−1 (Figure 1d) despite having low coulombic efficiencies (Figure S1).
The alteration of the voltage profiles of all electrolytes at various cycles is presented in Figures S2-S6.

Figure 2c shows that the discharge profile of the SL-LiClO4 electrolyte changes dramatically with the alteration of the E/S ratio.
In addition to a decreasing capacity with an increase in the electrolyte amount, the first plateaus are not seen clearly at the two highest E/S ratios.
In this regard, it can be said that at high E/S ratios, the formation of long LiPS chains in the sulfolane-based electrolytes is hindered [38].
The physicochemical and electrochemical properties of the electrolyte change along cycling.
During cycling, the dissolution of the polysulfides increases the viscosity of the electrolyte, influencing the ionic conductivity and wettability adversely [67, 68].
In addition, the thickness of the SEI layer and the precipitation of the species also change.
Correspondingly, the resistances within the cell are affected by these alterations, which influence the performance.
The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) method can give us information about these processes inside the cell [69–73].
In this regard, Li-S cells with the lowest E/S ratio were also characterized using the EIS method.
Figure 3 shows an example of the Z-fitting applied to the impedance spectra and the proposed equivalent circuit used in this characterization.
R1, R2, and R3 represent the electrolyte resistance, charge transfer resistance, and Li2S film resistance, respectively.
Q2 and Q3 are constant phase elements, whereas W1 is the Warburg diffusion resistance [55].
Figure 4 demonstrates the experimental impedance spectra for representative replicate cells with SL-LiTFSI, SL-LiTF, SL- LiClO4, G3-LiTFSI, and G3-LiTF electrolytes at an E/S ratio of 6 mL g−1.
For all electrolyte systems, two semicircles and a linear line describing the Warburg diffusion resistance are observed clearly.
The average results of the EIS can also be seen in Supporting Information (Table S1).

the total cell resistance of Li-S batteries with five different electrolytes for an E/S ratio of 6 mL g−1.
In Figure 5a, the highest electrolyte resistances, R1, are seen for G3-LiTF and SL-LiTF, indicating that the impact of LiTF salt on the electrolyte viscosity may be significant.
This may be why, in Figure 1d, the Li-S cell with G3-LiTF shows inferior capacities compared to others within the first few cycles.
On the other hand, the lowest electrolyte resistances are observed for LiTFSI-containing electrolytes at almost all cycles.
This indicates that the lithium salt type plays a significant role in the electrolyte resistance.

It is seen in Figure 5b that the lowest charge transfer resistances are obtained for SL-LiTFSI and SL-LiClO4, which is consistent with a previous study reporting that electrolytes containing LiClO4 exhibit the lowest charge transfer resistance among the electrolytes with LiTF and LiTFSI in DOL:DME [40].
It is also apparent that cells with SL-based electrolytes lead to better charge transfer kinetics.
In Figure 5c, the lowest film resistance is seen for SL- LiClO4, which may be related to the polysulfide dissolution kinetics in SL-LiClO4.
The total resistance of almost all cells peaks at the first cycle and then decreases slightly in Figure 5d.
After the third cycle, resistances remain almost constant.
As seen in Figure 1d, Li-S cells with SL-LiTFSI and SL-LiTF show the highest capacities within the first 10 cycles.
Figure 5d, presenting low cell resistances for SL-LiTFSI and SL-LiTF, supports the superiority of these electrolytes for the first few cycles.

Yet, as seen in the figure, the trend in the variance of total cell resistance with the electrolyte type is not entirely sufficient to explain the cycling performance seen in Figure 1d, as the Li-S cell with SL-LiClO4 showing the worst cycling performance presents the lowest total cell resistance.

Nevertheless, we may conclude that the composition of the electrolyte plays a significant role in the cell resistance because the morphology of the sulfur electrode, the polysulfide shuttle mechanism, and the conductivity affecting the resistance are all influenced by the electrochemical properties of the salt and solvent used in the electrolyte [74–76].
Figure 6 illustrates the cyclic voltammetry (CV) results of five different electrolyte systems at two E/S ratios, 9 and 6 mL g−1.

The typical CV curves of Li-S cells contain two reduction peaks at around 2.4–2.2 and 2.1–1.9 V, representing the reduction of solid S8 to long-chain lithium polysulfides Li2Sn (3≤n ≤ 8) and LiPSs to Li2S2/LiS2, respectively, which in turn show two discharge plateaus.
In addition to cathodic peaks, there are two oxidation peaks at anodic steps; however, oxidation peaks might overlap and be indistinguishable [77, 78].

When comparing two electrolyte amounts, two anodic and cathodic peaks are clear at an E/S ratio of 9, compared to 6 mL g−1, except for the G3-LiTF electrolyte, in which the oxidation peaks are overlapped, and the oxidation peak potentials are lowered.
Higher reduction peaks are observed as the electrolyte amount increases, demonstrating higher polysulfide conversion and enhanced redox kinetics as expected in Figure S7.

The alteration of the redox potentials is also evidenced by the voltage difference between charge and discharge curves in Figures S2–S6; generally, voltage hysteresis is higher for the E/S ratio of 6 mL g−1 than that of 9 mL g−1.

For an E/S ratio of 9 mL g−1, the reduction peaks of SL-based electrolytes are slightly higher than those of glymebased electrolytes, indicating that at this E/S ratio, sulfolanebased electrolytes are slightly more kinetically favorable.

The reduction peaks are similarly close to each other.

So it may be discussed that for lower E/S ratios, sulfolane-based electrolyte systems offer enhanced reaction kinetics and faster handling of polysulfide conversion; the CV peaks are distorted for the glyme-based electrolytes in lean electrolyte conditions.

Sulfur utilization is the measure of how close the high voltage capacity is to the theoretical high voltage capacity (418 mAh g−1), indicating the ability of active solid sulfur material present in the cathode to be turned into polysulfides dissolved in electrolyte.

On the other hand, the capacity ratio is the ratio of the low-voltage capacity to the high-voltage capacity, which has a theoretical value of 3, highlighting the reduction of longer-chain polysulfides to the final discharge product Li2S [79].
Figure S8 depicts the sulfur utilization and capacity ratio for different electrolyte systems for an E/S ratio of 6 mL g−1.
With the increase in the cycle number, sulfur utilization decreases, likely due to the loss of active material with polysulfide shuttling, electrode surface passivation, or side reactions.
Generally, sulfolane-based electrolytes have higher sulfur utilization than glyme-based electrolytes.
It can further be deduced that the higher sulfur utilization can also be beneficial for having higher system-level energy densities.
The SL-LiTFSI system outperforms other electrolyte systems, consistently demonstrating higher sulfur utilization across cycling.
As in the case of the capacity ratio, it increases slightly with an increase in the cycle number.

For glyme-based electrolyte systems, the capacity ratio is higher than that of sulfolane-based electrolytes, showing a higher reduction possibility of longer chain polysulfides to lower chain polysulfides.

Figure 7a-c shows the morphologies of the pristine lithium and lithium metal anode cycled in Li-S batteries with SL-LiTFSI and G3-LiTFSI electrolytes, demonstrating the best cycling performance at the lowest E/S ratio of 6 mL g−1.
Smooth surface morphology is observed in pristine lithium, whereas different morphological degradation, depending on the electrolyte type, is observed in the Li anode after 10 cycles.
In an ideal scenario, the SEI layer should be homogeneous, with low electronic and high ionic conductivity, formed due to electrolyte exposure.
But in Figure 7, there exist surface inhomogeneities that may cause a non-uniform current distribution and changes in the conductive properties of the electrode [80].
In the SL-based electrolyte, the lithium surface is relatively smoother and more compact than the G3-based electrolyte.
Nevertheless, localized degradation, indicative of heterogeneous deposition, is observed on the surface of the Li anode with an SL-based electrolyte.
In contrast, the cycled lithium anode with a G3-based electrolyte exhibits a more mossy, highly porous surface, indicating unstable lithium plating/stripping [81–84].
LiTFSI-containing electrolytes may lead to inhomogeneous surface morphology on the lithium metal anode.
Especially for the low-length glymes, this inhomogeneity may increase [80].
Moreover, Figure S9 shows the EDS mapping of the sulfur on the lithium surface.
More homogeneous and less intense sulfur accumulation on the Li surface is observed in the SL-based electrolyte.
A more pronounced sulfur accumulation in the G3-based electrolyte indicates that polysulfides are transported to the anode surface and react with Li metal.

According to the EDS results, the most prominent compounds in the SEI layer are expected to be lithium oxide (Li2O) and lithium carbonate (Li2CO3), with LiF present in smaller amounts [80].

The Nyquist plots obtained for the isothermal storage of symmetrical Li–Li cells containing SL or G3 electrolytes saturated with long-chain lithium polysulfides in Figure S13 and the cycling performance of these symmetrical Li–Li cells in Figure S14 also support the hypothesis that a more stable SEI layer formation occurs for SL-based electrolytes, indicating that SL-based electrolytes are promising for Li-S batteries. 3 | Experimental The carbon-sulfur composite cathode was prepared first, adjusting the weight percentages of sulfur, carbon (Super C65), and binder (PVDF) as 60, 30, and 10, respectively, corresponding to a carbon-to-sulfur ratio of 0.5.
The obtained sulfur loading was 1.1–1.3 mg cm−2, and 2.01 cm2 cathode disks were used.
Before the preparation of the electrolytes, sulfolane and triglyme solvents were dried by molecular sieves (0.4 nm, Sigma Aldrich), which were freshly calcined.
Then, dried solvents were mixed with the required amounts of salts with a magnetic stirrer overnight in a glovebox (MBraun) in which the humidity and oxygen contents were less than 0.5 ppm.
Five different electrolyte systems were prepared: 1 M LiTFSI, 1 M LiTF, or 1 M LiClO4 in sulfolane and 1 M LiTFSI or 1 M LiTF in triglyme.
To assemble CR2032-type coin cells, metallic lithium anode (2.01 cm2, 170 μm) and polymeric Celgard (3.01 cm2, 25 μm) separators were used under an inert atmosphere.
Cells with different E/S ratios of 6, 9, 16, and 23 mL g−1 were prepared for different types of electrolytes, keeping other parameters such as the sulfur loading and carbon-to-sulfur ratio constant.
The prepared cells were kept at the open circuit voltage (OCV) for 16 h for stabilization.
Galvanostatic cycling was carried out at room temperature by a Neware battery cycler.
After resting, each cell was cycled at 0.1 Crate between cut-off voltages of 1.5–2.8 V.
For the EIS measurements, cells again rested at the OCV for 16 h.

Then, at the end of the rest period and the end of the first, third, fifth, eighth, and tenth discharge, the EIS measurements were conducted within 10 mHz to 1 MHz, with a 10 mV amplitude using Biologic SP 300/300e.
Before each EIS measurement, cells rested for 30 min for equilibration.
In the EIS characterization, the lowest E/S ratio, 6 mL g−1, was chosen since we are particularly interested in low E/S ratios for practical Li-S batteries.
Experiments were conducted with at least three replicates, and the results were reported as averages of replicates.
CV analysis was performed between 1.5 and 3.0 V with a scan rate of 0.1 mV s−1 by using Biologic SP 300/300e.

The lithium electrodes for morphological characterization were obtained by disassembling the cells in a glovebox and rinsing them with DME to remove loosely bound compounds and lithium salts; they were then dried overnight under an inert atmosphere.
They were transferred to the SEM in vacuum containers.

The electrode morphologies were characterized using a scanning electron microscope (SEM; Thermo Scientific, Quattro S), and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) analysis was conducted with the SEM system. 4 | Conclusion The impact of the E/S ratio on the electrochemical performance of Li-S batteries with various electrolyte systems was analyzed. 1 M LiTFSI and 1 M LiTF salts in sulfolane and triglyme solvents, and 1 M LiClO4 salt in sulfolane electrolyte systems were tested for E/S ratios of 6, 9, 16, and 23 mL g−1.
SL-LiTFSI and G3-LiTFSI electrolytes exhibit superior cycling performance compared to others across various E/S ratios, owing to the exceptional cycling stability and rate capability of LiTFSI.

However, at the lowest E/S ratio of 6 mL g−1, the Li-S cell with SL-LiTFSI demonstrates better cycling performance than G3-LiTFSI, likely due to the electrochemical stability, high dielectric constant, and donor number of sulfolane.
Yet, G3-LiTF exhibits the highest discharge capacity and capacity retention at the lowest E/S ratio of 6 mL g−1 across all electrolytes despite suffering from low CE.
EIS measurements reveal two semicircles and a linear line, indicative of Warburg diffusion resistance, across all electrolytes.
The total cell resistance peaks in the initial cycle and slightly decreases afterward.
CV analysis of Li-S cells and morphological investigations of Li anodes cycled with different electrolyte systems also enriched our mechanistic analysis.

Overall, the impact of the E/S ratio on discharge capacity and cycling performance varies among different electrolyte systems, highlighting the significant role of the solvent and its combination with lithium salts in battery performance.
Designing electrolytes for optimal performance under lean electrolyte conditions is crucial for achieving highperformance Li-S batteries.
Notably, the 1 M LiTFSI in sulfolane electrolyte system shows promise, demonstrating superior cycling performance at the lowest E/S ratio.
